lessons.title: What is Query Optimization?
lessons.content: Query optimization improves performance by selecting the best execution plan. Example: Use EXPLAIN to analyze SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE CustomerID = 101;

lessons.title: Using EXPLAIN
lessons.content: EXPLAIN shows the query plan. Example: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE Total > 1000; reveals index usage and scan types (PostgreSQL/MySQL).

lessons.title: Cost-Based Optimization
lessons.content: DBMS uses cost estimates to choose plans. Lower cost means faster execution. Example: Indexes reduce cost for WHERE clauses.

lessons.question: What does the DBMS use to choose query plans?

lessons.title: Avoiding Table Scans
lessons.content: Full table scans are slow for large tables. Example: Add an index on CustomerID to optimize SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE CustomerID = 101;

lessons.question: What can a full table scan cause?

lessons.title: Join Optimization
lessons.content: Optimize joins with indexes and smaller tables first. Example: SELECT c.Name, o.Total FROM Customers c JOIN Orders o ON c.CustomerID = o.CustomerID; benefits from indexes.

lessons.title: Query Rewriting
lessons.content: Rewrite subqueries as joins. Example: Rewrite SELECT * FROM Products WHERE Price > (SELECT AVG(Price) FROM Products) as a JOIN for better performance.

lessons.question: What can be faster than a subquery?

lessons.title: Statistics and Updates
lessons.content: DBMS relies on statistics for optimization. Example: ANALYZE TABLE Orders; updates stats for better plans (PostgreSQL/MySQL).

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: Query optimization is critical for large datasets, reporting, and high-concurrency systems.

lessons.title: What Are Indexes?
lessons.content: Indexes speed up queries by storing sorted data. Example: CREATE INDEX idx_customer ON Orders (CustomerID);

lessons.title: Covering Indexes
lessons.content: Covering indexes include all query columns. Example: CREATE INDEX idx_order_cover ON Orders (CustomerID, Total); for SELECT CustomerID, Total FROM Orders;

lessons.title: Partial Indexes
lessons.content: Partial indexes cover a subset of rows. Example: CREATE INDEX idx_active ON Customers (CustomerID) WHERE Active = 1; (PostgreSQL).

lessons.question: What does a partial index cover?

lessons.title: Composite Indexes
lessons.content: Composite indexes include multiple columns. Example: CREATE INDEX idx_composite ON Orders (CustomerID, OrderDate);

lessons.title: Index Maintenance
lessons.content: Rebuild indexes to reduce fragmentation. Example: REINDEX TABLE Orders; (PostgreSQL) or ALTER INDEX idx_customer REBUILD; (SQL Server).

lessons.title: Performance Trade-offs
lessons.content: Indexes speed up SELECT but slow INSERT/UPDATE. Balance index creation with write performance.

lessons.title: Choosing Columns
lessons.content: Index columns used in WHERE, JOIN, or ORDER BY. Example: Index OrderDate for SELECT * FROM Orders ORDER BY OrderDate;

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: Indexes are critical for large tables, frequent queries, and performance-sensitive applications.

lessons.title: What Are Transactions?
lessons.content: Transactions ensure data consistency with ACID properties. Example: BEGIN TRANSACTION; UPDATE Accounts SET Balance = Balance - 100 WHERE ID = 1; COMMIT;

lessons.title: Savepoints
lessons.content: Savepoints allow partial rollbacks. Example: BEGIN; UPDATE Orders SET Total = 100; SAVEPOINT sp1; UPDATE Orders SET Total = 200; ROLLBACK TO sp1; COMMIT;

lessons.title: Isolation Levels
lessons.content: Isolation levels control concurrency. Example: SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED; (options: READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE).

lessons.title: Nested Transactions
lessons.content: Some DBMS support nested transactions via savepoints. Example: BEGIN; SAVEPOINT sp1; UPDATE Orders SET Total = 100; SAVEPOINT sp2; ROLLBACK TO sp2;

lessons.question: How are nested transactions often implemented?

lessons.title: Transaction Rollback
lessons.content: ROLLBACK undoes changes. Example: BEGIN; UPDATE Accounts SET Balance = Balance - 100; ROLLBACK; leaves Balance unchanged.

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Keep transactions short to reduce locking and improve concurrency.

lessons.title: Error Handling
lessons.content: Use TRY-CATCH in transactions to handle errors. Example: BEGIN TRY; UPDATE Orders; COMMIT; END TRY BEGIN CATCH; ROLLBACK; END CATCH; (SQL Server).

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: Complex transactions are used for financial operations, inventory updates, and multi-step data changes.

lessons.title: What is Dynamic SQL?
lessons.content: Dynamic SQL builds and executes SQL at runtime. Example: SET @sql = 'SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE Total > ' + CAST(@threshold AS VARCHAR); EXEC(@sql); (SQL Server).

lessons.title: Using EXECUTE
lessons.content: EXECUTE runs dynamic SQL. Example: EXECUTE ('SELECT * FROM ' + @tableName); (PostgreSQL: EXECUTE format('SELECT * FROM %I', tableName)).

lessons.title: Parameterized Dynamic SQL
lessons.content: Use parameters to avoid injection. Example: EXEC sp_executesql @sql, N'@threshold INT', @threshold = 1000; (SQL Server).

lessons.question: What prevents SQL injection in dynamic SQL?

lessons.title: Building Queries
lessons.content: Concatenate strings for flexibility. Example: SET @sql = 'SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE ' + @condition; EXEC(@sql);

lessons.title: Dynamic Table Names
lessons.content: Use dynamic SQL for variable table names. Example: EXECUTE format('SELECT * FROM %I', @tableName); (PostgreSQL).

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Dynamic SQL may bypass query plan caching. Use parameterized queries to improve performance.

lessons.question: What can improve dynamic SQL performance?

lessons.title: Security Risks
lessons.content: Avoid concatenating user input directly to prevent SQL injection. Always use parameters.

lessons.question: What does concatenating user input risk?

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: Dynamic SQL is used for flexible reports, dynamic table operations, and automated scripts.

lessons.title: Recursive CTEs
lessons.content: Recursive CTEs handle hierarchies. Example: WITH RECURSIVE Tree AS (SELECT EmployeeID, Name, ManagerID FROM Employees WHERE ManagerID IS NULL UNION ALL SELECT e.EmployeeID, e.Name, e.ManagerID FROM Employees e JOIN Tree t ON e.ManagerID = t.EmployeeID) SELECT * FROM Tree;

lessons.title: Recursive CTE Structure
lessons.content: Recursive CTEs use UNION ALL with a base case and recursive step. Example: Base case selects root, recursive step joins to CTE.

lessons.question: What connects base and recursive steps in a CTE?

lessons.title: Depth Control
lessons.content: Limit recursion with a condition. Example: Add WHERE depth < 5 to recursive CTE to limit hierarchy levels.

lessons.question: How can you limit recursion in a CTE?

lessons.title: Path Tracking
lessons.content: Track hierarchy paths. Example: WITH RECURSIVE Tree AS (...) SELECT Name, CONCAT(t.Path, ' -> ', t.Name) AS Path FROM Tree t;

lessons.question: What can CONCAT do in a recursive CTE?

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Recursive CTEs can be slow for deep hierarchies. Ensure indexes on join columns like ManagerID.

lessons.title: Cycle Detection
lessons.content: Prevent infinite loops with cycle detection. Example: Use CYCLE clause in PostgreSQL to detect repeated EmployeeIDs.

lessons.question: What prevents infinite loops in recursive CTEs?

lessons.title: Non-Recursive CTEs
lessons.content: Advanced non-recursive CTEs simplify complex joins. Example: WITH Sales AS (SELECT CustomerID, SUM(Total) FROM Orders GROUP BY CustomerID) SELECT * FROM Sales JOIN Customers;

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: Recursive CTEs are used for organizational charts, bill of materials, or graph traversals.

lessons.title: Custom Window Frames
lessons.content: Define precise window frames with ROWS or RANGE. Example: SELECT OrderID, SUM(Total) OVER (PARTITION BY CustomerID ORDER BY OrderDate ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS RecentSum FROM Orders;

lessons.question: What does ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW define?

lessons.title: RANGE vs. ROWS
lessons.content: RANGE considers value ranges, ROWS considers row counts. Example: RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '1' DAY PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW for date-based windows.

lessons.question: What does RANGE use for window frames?

lessons.title: CUME_DIST()
lessons.content: CUME_DIST() calculates cumulative distribution. Example: SELECT Name, CUME_DIST() OVER (ORDER BY Price) AS Dist FROM Products;

lessons.title: PERCENT_RANK()
lessons.content: PERCENT_RANK() gives relative rank as a percentage. Example: SELECT Name, PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Price) AS Rank FROM Products;

lessons.title: Combining Window Functions
lessons.content: Use multiple window functions. Example: SELECT Name, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY Category ORDER BY Price), SUM(Price) OVER (PARTITION BY Category) FROM Products;

lessons.question: Can multiple window functions be combined?

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Complex window functions require sorting. Index PARTITION BY and ORDER BY columns for efficiency.

lessons.title: NULL Handling
lessons.content: Window functions like CUME_DIST() treat NULLs as values, sorted per ORDER BY rules.

lessons.question: How do window functions handle NULLs?

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: Expert window functions are used for advanced analytics, like moving averages or percentile rankings.

lessons.title: What is Table Partitioning?
lessons.content: Partitioning splits large tables into smaller parts. Example: CREATE TABLE Orders (OrderID INT, OrderDate DATE) PARTITION BY RANGE (OrderDate); (PostgreSQL).

lessons.title: Range Partitioning
lessons.content: Partition by ranges (e.g., dates). Example: PARTITION BY RANGE (OrderDate) (PARTITION p0 VALUES LESS THAN ('2023-01-01'), PARTITION p1 VALUES LESS THAN ('2024-01-01'));

lessons.title: List Partitioning
lessons.content: Partition by specific values. Example: PARTITION BY LIST (Region) (PARTITION p0 VALUES IN ('East'), PARTITION p1 VALUES IN ('West'));

lessons.title: Hash Partitioning
lessons.content: Partition by hash for even distribution. Example: PARTITION BY HASH (CustomerID) PARTITIONS 4;

lessons.title: Querying Partitions
lessons.content: Queries automatically target relevant partitions. Example: SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE OrderDate = '2023-06-01'; uses partition p0.

lessons.question: What do queries target in partitioned tables?

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Partitioning improves query speed for large tables but increases maintenance overhead.

lessons.question: What does partitioning improve for large tables?

lessons.title: Maintenance
lessons.content: Manage partitions with ADD/DROP. Example: ALTER TABLE Orders ADD PARTITION p2 VALUES LESS THAN ('2025-01-01');

lessons.question: How do you add a partition?

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: Partitioning is used for large datasets, like time-series data or regional sales, to improve performance.

lessons.title: What Are Materialized Views?
lessons.content: Materialized views store query results physically. Example: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW SalesSummary AS SELECT Category, SUM(Total) FROM Orders GROUP BY Category; (PostgreSQL).

lessons.title: Creating Materialized Views
lessons.content: Use CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW. Example: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW TopCustomers AS SELECT CustomerID, COUNT(*) FROM Orders GROUP BY CustomerID;

lessons.title: Refreshing Views
lessons.content: Refresh with REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW. Example: REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW SalesSummary; (use CONCURRENTLY in PostgreSQL to avoid locks).

lessons.title: Indexes on Views
lessons.content: Add indexes to materialized views. Example: CREATE INDEX idx_sales ON SalesSummary (Category);

lessons.question: Can indexes be added to materialized views?

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Materialized views speed up queries but require refreshes, which can be slow for large datasets.

lessons.question: What can slow materialized view refreshes?

lessons.title: Regular vs. Materialized Views
lessons.content: Regular views are virtual; materialized views store data. Materialized views need explicit refreshes.

lessons.question: What is a key difference between regular and materialized views?

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: Materialized views are used for precomputed aggregates, dashboards, or caching complex query results.

lessons.question: What are materialized views used for?

lessons.title: DBMS Support
lessons.content: Supported in PostgreSQL, Oracle; SQL Server uses indexed views. Check DBMS documentation.

lessons.title: Multi-Event Triggers
lessons.content: Triggers can handle multiple events. Example: CREATE TRIGGER Audit ON Orders FOR INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE AS INSERT INTO AuditLog (Action) VALUES ('Modified'); (SQL Server).

lessons.title: Conditional Logic
lessons.content: Use IF in triggers. Example: CREATE TRIGGER CheckPrice BEFORE INSERT ON Products FOR EACH ROW IF NEW.Price < 0 THEN SIGNAL SQLSTATE '45000'; END IF; (MySQL).

lessons.question: What allows conditional logic in triggers?

lessons.title: INSTEAD OF Triggers
lessons.content: INSTEAD OF triggers replace actions. Example: CREATE TRIGGER InsteadInsert INSTEAD OF INSERT ON ViewName FOR EACH ROW INSERT INTO BaseTable ...; (SQL Server).

lessons.question: What do INSTEAD OF triggers do?

lessons.title: Trigger Order
lessons.content: Some DBMS allow trigger order. Example: ALTER TRIGGER Audit FIRST AFTER INSERT ON Orders; (PostgreSQL).

lessons.question: Can trigger execution order be set?

lessons.title: Recursive Triggers
lessons.content: Triggers can cause recursion. Example: UPDATE in a trigger triggers another. Enable with ALTER DATABASE (SQL Server).

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Complex triggers slow operations. Keep logic minimal and avoid recursive triggers.

lessons.title: Debugging Triggers
lessons.content: Log trigger actions to debug. Example: INSERT INTO DebugLog (Message) VALUES (NEW.Price); in a trigger.

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: Advanced triggers enforce complex rules, audit changes, or update related tables.

lessons.title: Error Handling
lessons.content: Use TRY-CATCH in procedures. Example: CREATE PROCEDURE SafeUpdate AS BEGIN TRY UPDATE Orders SET Total = Total + 100; END TRY BEGIN CATCH ROLLBACK; END CATCH; (SQL Server).

lessons.question: What handles errors in stored procedures?

lessons.title: Cursors
lessons.content: Cursors process rows individually. Example: DECLARE cur CURSOR FOR SELECT CustomerID FROM Orders; OPEN cur; FETCH NEXT FROM cur; (SQL Server).

lessons.title: Dynamic SQL in Procedures
lessons.content: Use dynamic SQL for flexibility. Example: CREATE PROCEDURE DynamicQuery (@table VARCHAR(50)) AS EXEC('SELECT * FROM ' + @table);

lessons.question: What does dynamic SQL add to procedures?

lessons.title: Output Parameters
lessons.content: Return multiple values. Example: CREATE PROCEDURE GetStats (OUT total DECIMAL, OUT count INT) AS SELECT SUM(Total), COUNT(*) INTO total, count FROM Orders;

lessons.title: Temporary Tables
lessons.content: Use temp tables in procedures. Example: CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE #Temp (ID INT); INSERT INTO #Temp SELECT CustomerID FROM Orders;

lessons.question: Can temporary tables be used in procedures?

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Avoid cursors when possible; use set-based operations for better performance.

lessons.title: Security
lessons.content: Use EXECUTE AS to control permissions. Example: CREATE PROCEDURE GetData WITH EXECUTE AS OWNER AS SELECT * FROM Orders;

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: Advanced procedures handle complex logic, batch processing, or dynamic reporting.

lessons.title: What Are UDFs?
lessons.content: UDFs are custom functions returning values. Example: CREATE FUNCTION GetTax (@amount DECIMAL) RETURNS DECIMAL AS BEGIN RETURN @amount * 0.08; END; (SQL Server).

lessons.title: Scalar UDFs
lessons.content: Return a single value. Example: CREATE FUNCTION AddTax (@price DECIMAL) RETURNS DECIMAL AS RETURN @price * 1.1;

lessons.question: What does a scalar UDF return?

lessons.title: Table-Valued UDFs
lessons.content: Return a table. Example: CREATE FUNCTION GetOrders (@custID INT) RETURNS TABLE AS RETURN SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE CustomerID = @custID;

lessons.question: What does a table-valued UDF return?

lessons.title: Using UDFs
lessons.content: Call UDFs in queries. Example: SELECT ProductID, GetTax(Price) AS Tax FROM Products;

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Scalar UDFs can be slow in row-by-row operations. Consider inline table-valued UDFs for better performance.

lessons.question: What is faster than scalar UDFs?

lessons.title: Deterministic UDFs
lessons.content: Deterministic UDFs always return the same result for the same input. Example: GetTax() is deterministic.

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: UDFs are used for reusable calculations, like tax computations or custom filtering.

lessons.title: DBMS Support
lessons.content: UDFs are supported in SQL Server, PostgreSQL, Oracle; syntax varies. Check documentation.

lessons.title: What is SQL Injection?
lessons.content: SQL injection is a security vulnerability where malicious SQL is inserted. Example: Input ' OR '1'='1 can bypass WHERE clauses.

lessons.title: Parameterized Queries
lessons.content: Use parameters to prevent injection. Example: PREPARE stmt FROM 'SELECT * FROM Users WHERE ID = ?'; EXECUTE stmt USING @id; (MySQL).

lessons.title: Escaping Inputs
lessons.content: Escape special characters if parameters aren’t possible. Example: Use QUOTE() in MySQL to escape strings.

lessons.question: What can be used if parameters aren’t possible?

lessons.title: Avoiding Concatenation
lessons.content: Don’t concatenate user input in dynamic SQL. Example: Avoid SET @sql = 'SELECT * FROM Users WHERE Name = ''' + @name + '''';

lessons.question: What should you avoid in dynamic SQL?

lessons.title: Stored Procedures
lessons.content: Use stored procedures with parameters. Example: CREATE PROCEDURE GetUser (@id INT) AS SELECT * FROM Users WHERE ID = @id;

lessons.question: How do stored procedures help prevent injection?

lessons.title: Input Validation
lessons.content: Validate inputs before use. Example: Check if input is numeric before using in WHERE ID = input;

lessons.question: What should you do before using inputs?

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: SQL injection prevention is critical for web applications, APIs, and any user-facing database.

lessons.question: Where is SQL injection prevention critical?

lessons.title: Tools
lessons.content: Use ORMs or libraries that handle parameterization, like SQLAlchemy for Python.

lessons.title: What Are Database Locks?
lessons.content: Locks prevent concurrent data changes. Example: SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE ID = 1 FOR UPDATE; locks rows (PostgreSQL).

lessons.title: Row-Level Locks
lessons.content: Lock specific rows. Example: SELECT * FROM Accounts WHERE ID = 101 FOR UPDATE; prevents updates to that row.

lessons.title: Table-Level Locks
lessons.content: Lock entire tables. Example: LOCK TABLE Orders IN EXCLUSIVE MODE; (PostgreSQL).

lessons.title: Deadlocks
lessons.content: Deadlocks occur when transactions wait for each other. Example: Transaction A locks row 1, B locks row 2, each waits for the other.

lessons.title: Avoiding Deadlocks
lessons.content: Access resources in a consistent order. Example: Always lock Orders before Customers in transactions.

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Minimize lock duration with short transactions to improve concurrency.

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: Locks are critical for financial systems, inventory, or any concurrent data updates.

lessons.title: MVCC
lessons.content: Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) avoids locks by using versions. Supported in PostgreSQL, Oracle.

lessons.title: Time Zones
lessons.content: Handle time zones. Example: SELECT NOW() AT TIME ZONE 'UTC'; (PostgreSQL) or CONVERT_TZ(NOW(), 'UTC', 'EST'); (MySQL).

lessons.question: What does AT TIME ZONE do?

lessons.title: Date Arithmetic
lessons.content: Add/subtract intervals. Example: SELECT OrderDate + INTERVAL '30 days' AS DueDate FROM Orders; (PostgreSQL).

lessons.title: Date Formatting
lessons.content: Format dates. Example: SELECT TO_CHAR(OrderDate, 'YYYY-MM-DD') FROM Orders; (PostgreSQL) or DATE_FORMAT(OrderDate, '%Y-%m-%d') (MySQL).

lessons.question: What does EXTRACT(YEAR FROM OrderDate) do?

lessons.title: Interval Calculations
lessons.content: Calculate time differences. Example: SELECT AGE(OrderDate, '2023-01-01') AS TimeSince FROM Orders; (PostgreSQL).

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Index date columns for range queries. Example: CREATE INDEX idx_date ON Orders (OrderDate);

lessons.question: What improves date range query performance?

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: Date operations are used for scheduling, reporting, or time-series analysis.

lessons.question: What are date operations used for?

lessons.title: DBMS Variations
lessons.content: Date functions vary. PostgreSQL uses TO_CHAR, MySQL uses DATE_FORMAT, SQL Server uses FORMAT.

lessons.title: What Are Regular Expressions?
lessons.content: Regular expressions match patterns. Example: SELECT * FROM Customers WHERE Name ~ '^[A-Z]'; matches names starting with a capital letter (PostgreSQL).

lessons.title: Using REGEXP
lessons.content: Use REGEXP or ~. Example: SELECT * FROM Products WHERE Name REGEXP 'phone$'; matches names ending with 'phone' (MySQL).

lessons.title: Character Classes
lessons.content: Use [A-Z], [0-9], etc. Example: SELECT * FROM Customers WHERE Email ~ '[a-z0-9]+@'; matches valid email patterns (PostgreSQL).

lessons.title: Anchors
lessons.content: Use ^ and $ for start/end. Example: SELECT * FROM Products WHERE Code ~ '^[A-Z]{3}$'; matches 3-letter codes (PostgreSQL).

lessons.question: What does ^ in a regex do?

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Regex queries may not use indexes. Use LIKE for simple patterns if possible.

lessons.question: What can be faster than REGEXP for simple patterns?

lessons.title: DBMS Support
lessons.content: PostgreSQL uses ~, MySQL uses REGEXP, SQL Server uses PATINDEX. Check documentation.

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: Regex is used for validating emails, phone numbers, or complex string patterns.

lessons.title: Replacing Patterns
lessons.content: Replace with REGEXP_REPLACE. Example: SELECT REGEXP_REPLACE(Name, '[0-9]', '') FROM Customers; removes digits (PostgreSQL).

lessons.title: Querying JSON
lessons.content: Query JSON data. Example: SELECT Data->>'name' AS Name FROM Users WHERE Data->>'age' > '30'; (PostgreSQL, JSONB column).

lessons.title: JSON Functions
lessons.content: Use JSON functions. Example: SELECT JSON_EXTRACT(Data, '$.name') FROM Users; (MySQL).

lessons.title: Querying XML
lessons.content: Query XML data. Example: SELECT XMLQUERY('//name/text()' PASSING Data) FROM Users; (Oracle).

lessons.title: JSONB vs. JSON
lessons.content: JSONB (PostgreSQL) stores binary JSON, enabling indexing. Example: CREATE INDEX idx_json ON Users USING GIN (Data);

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Index JSON fields for faster queries. Example: CREATE INDEX ON Users (Data->>'name'); (PostgreSQL).

lessons.title: Modifying JSON
lessons.content: Update JSON. Example: UPDATE Users SET Data = JSON_SET(Data, '$.age', 31) WHERE ID = 1; (MySQL).

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: JSON/XML are used for semi-structured data, like user profiles or API responses.

lessons.title: DBMS Support
lessons.content: JSON in PostgreSQL (JSONB), MySQL, SQL Server; XML in Oracle, SQL Server. Syntax varies.

lessons.title: Optimizing CTEs
lessons.content: CTEs may not be materialized. Example: WITH Sales AS (SELECT * FROM Orders) SELECT * FROM Sales WHERE Total > 1000; may re-run the CTE.

lessons.title: Materializing CTEs
lessons.content: Use temp tables for materialization. Example: CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE TempSales AS SELECT * FROM Orders; SELECT * FROM TempSales;

lessons.title: Recursive CTE Performance
lessons.content: Optimize recursive CTEs with indexes. Example: Index ManagerID for WITH RECURSIVE Tree AS (...) SELECT * FROM Employees;

lessons.title: Avoiding Redundant CTEs
lessons.content: Reuse CTEs instead of repeating. Example: WITH Data AS (SELECT * FROM Orders) SELECT * FROM Data UNION SELECT * FROM Data;

lessons.title: CTEs vs. Subqueries
lessons.content: CTEs improve readability but may not optimize better than subqueries. Test with EXPLAIN.

lessons.question: What should you test CTE performance with?

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Limit CTE complexity and use indexes on joined or filtered columns.

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: Optimized CTEs are used for hierarchical queries, multi-step calculations, or readable joins.

lessons.question: What are optimized CTEs used for?

lessons.title: DBMS Variations
lessons.content: PostgreSQL, SQL Server support CTEs; MySQL supports since 8.0. Check documentation.

lessons.title: Dynamic Pivoting
lessons.content: Use dynamic SQL for pivoting. Example: SET @sql = (SELECT GROUP_CONCAT('SUM(CASE WHEN Month = ''' || Month || ''' THEN Sales END) AS ' || Month) FROM Months); EXEC(@sql); (MySQL).

lessons.question: What is used for dynamic pivoting?

lessons.title: Cross-Tab Reports
lessons.content: Create cross-tab reports with CASE. Example: SELECT Category, SUM(CASE WHEN Month = 'Jan' THEN Sales END) AS Jan FROM Orders GROUP BY Category;

lessons.title: Dynamic Unpivoting
lessons.content: Unpivot dynamically. Example: SET @sql = 'SELECT * FROM SalesTable UNPIVOT (Sales FOR Month IN (' + @months + '))'; EXEC(@sql);

lessons.question: What is used for dynamic unpivoting?

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Dynamic pivoting can be slow. Precompute results in materialized views if possible.

lessons.question: What can improve dynamic pivoting performance?

lessons.title: NULL Handling
lessons.content: Use COALESCE for NULLs. Example: SELECT Category, COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN Month = 'Jan' THEN Sales END), 0) AS Jan FROM Orders GROUP BY Category;

lessons.title: DBMS Support
lessons.content: PIVOT in SQL Server, Oracle; MySQL uses CASE. Dynamic pivoting requires dynamic SQL.

lessons.question: Which DBMS requires CASE for pivoting?

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: Advanced pivoting is used for dynamic reports, like sales by month or region.

lessons.question: What are advanced pivoting reports used for?

lessons.title: Automation
lessons.content: Automate pivoting with stored procedures to generate column lists dynamically.

lessons.title: What is Full-Text Search?
lessons.content: Full-text search finds text patterns. Example: SELECT * FROM Products WHERE to_tsvector(Name) @@ to_tsquery('phone'); (PostgreSQL).

lessons.title: TSVECTOR and TSQUERY
lessons.content: Use TSVECTOR for indexing, TSQUERY for searching. Example: SELECT * FROM Products WHERE to_tsvector(Name) @@ to_tsquery('phone & tablet'); (PostgreSQL).

lessons.title: Full-Text Indexes
lessons.content: Create full-text indexes. Example: CREATE INDEX idx_fts ON Products USING GIN (to_tsvector('english', Name)); (PostgreSQL).

lessons.title: Ranking Results
lessons.content: Rank search results. Example: SELECT Name, ts_rank(to_tsvector(Name), to_tsquery('phone')) AS Rank FROM Products; (PostgreSQL).

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Use GIN indexes for full-text search to avoid slow scans.

lessons.question: What index type is used for full-text search?

lessons.title: DBMS Support
lessons.content: PostgreSQL uses TSVECTOR; SQL Server uses CONTAINS; MySQL uses MATCH. Check documentation.

lessons.question: Which DBMS uses MATCH for full-text search?

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: Full-text search is used for product searches, document retrieval, or content management.

lessons.question: What is full-text search used for?

lessons.title: Stemming
lessons.content: Stemming matches word variations. Example: 'phone' matches 'phones' in to_tsquery('phone').

lessons.title: What Are Database Statistics?
lessons.content: Statistics help the optimizer choose plans. Example: ANALYZE Orders; updates stats (PostgreSQL/MySQL).

lessons.title: Updating Statistics
lessons.content: Update stats after data changes. Example: UPDATE STATISTICS Orders; (SQL Server).

lessons.title: Vacuuming
lessons.content: Vacuum cleans dead rows. Example: VACUUM ANALYZE Orders; (PostgreSQL) reclaims space and updates stats.

lessons.title: Rebuilding Indexes
lessons.content: Rebuild fragmented indexes. Example: REINDEX TABLE Orders; (PostgreSQL) or ALTER INDEX idx_orders REBUILD; (SQL Server).

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Schedule maintenance during low activity to avoid locking.

lessons.title: Monitoring Statistics
lessons.content: Check stats staleness. Example: SELECT * FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname = 'Orders'; (PostgreSQL).

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: Statistics and maintenance ensure optimal query performance in large databases.

lessons.title: Automation
lessons.content: Automate maintenance with jobs. Example: PostgreSQL’s autovacuum or SQL Server Agent.

lessons.title: What is RBAC?
lessons.content: Role-Based Access Control manages permissions via roles. Example: CREATE ROLE analyst; GRANT SELECT ON Orders TO analyst; (PostgreSQL).

lessons.title: Creating Roles
lessons.content: Create roles. Example: CREATE ROLE report_user WITH LOGIN PASSWORD 'secure'; (PostgreSQL).

lessons.title: Granting Permissions
lessons.content: Grant specific permissions. Example: GRANT INSERT, UPDATE ON Orders TO report_user;

lessons.title: Revoking Permissions
lessons.content: Revoke access. Example: REVOKE INSERT ON Orders FROM report_user;

lessons.title: Role Inheritance
lessons.content: Roles can inherit permissions. Example: GRANT analyst TO report_user; (PostgreSQL).

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Simplify role hierarchies to reduce permission check overhead.

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: RBAC is used for secure access in multi-user systems, like enterprise databases.

lessons.title: Auditing Roles
lessons.content: Audit permissions. Example: SELECT * FROM information_schema.table_privileges WHERE table_name = 'Orders';

lessons.title: TRY-CATCH Blocks
lessons.content: Handle errors with TRY-CATCH. Example: BEGIN TRY INSERT INTO Orders VALUES (NULL); END TRY BEGIN CATCH SELECT ERROR_MESSAGE(); END CATCH; (SQL Server).

lessons.question: What handles errors in SQL Server?

lessons.title: Custom Errors
lessons.content: Raise custom errors. Example: RAISE EXCEPTION 'Invalid price' USING ERRCODE = '22000'; (PostgreSQL).

lessons.question: What raises custom errors in PostgreSQL?

lessons.title: Error Logging
lessons.content: Log errors to a table. Example: INSERT INTO ErrorLog (Error) SELECT ERROR_MESSAGE() FROM CATCH; (SQL Server).

lessons.question: What can errors be logged to?

lessons.title: Transaction Rollback
lessons.content: Rollback on error. Example: BEGIN TRY BEGIN TRANSACTION; INSERT INTO Orders; COMMIT; END TRY BEGIN CATCH ROLLBACK; END CATCH;

lessons.question: What does CATCH do on error?

lessons.title: Error Details
lessons.content: Retrieve error details. Example: SELECT ERROR_LINE(), ERROR_NUMBER() FROM CATCH; (SQL Server).

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Minimize TRY-CATCH overhead by using in critical sections only.

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: Error handling is used for robust procedures, transaction safety, and debugging.

lessons.question: What is error handling used for?

lessons.title: DBMS Variations
lessons.content: SQL Server uses TRY-CATCH; PostgreSQL uses EXCEPTION; MySQL uses DECLARE HANDLER.

lessons.title: What Are Temporal Tables?
lessons.content: Temporal tables track history. Example: CREATE TABLE Employees (ID INT, Name VARCHAR(50), SysStartTime DATETIME2 GENERATED ALWAYS AS ROW START, SysEndTime DATETIME2 GENERATED ALWAYS AS ROW END, PERIOD FOR SYSTEM_TIME (SysStartTime, SysEndTime)) WITH (SYSTEM_VERSIONING = ON); (SQL Server).

lessons.title: Querying History
lessons.content: Query historical data. Example: SELECT * FROM Employees FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF '2023-01-01'; (SQL Server).

lessons.question: What does FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF do?

lessons.title: History Table
lessons.content: History is stored in a separate table. Example: WITH (SYSTEM_VERSIONING = ON (HISTORY_TABLE = EmployeesHistory));

lessons.question: Where is temporal table history stored?

lessons.title: Enabling Temporal
lessons.content: Enable with SYSTEM_VERSIONING. Example: ALTER TABLE Employees SET (SYSTEM_VERSIONING = ON);

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Index history tables for faster queries. Example: CREATE INDEX idx_history ON EmployeesHistory (SysStartTime);

lessons.question: What improves temporal table query performance?

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: Temporal tables are used for auditing, compliance, or tracking data changes over time.

lessons.question: What are temporal tables used for?

lessons.title: DBMS Support
lessons.content: SQL Server, Oracle support temporal tables; PostgreSQL uses triggers for similar functionality.

lessons.question: Which DBMS natively supports temporal tables?

lessons.title: Retention
lessons.content: Set history retention. Example: ALTER TABLE Employees SET (SYSTEM_VERSIONING = ON (HISTORY_RETENTION_PERIOD = 1 YEAR));

lessons.title: What is Query Parallelism?
lessons.content: Query parallelism splits queries across multiple CPU cores. Example: SELECT /*+ PARALLEL(4) */ SUM(Total) FROM Orders; (Oracle) enables 4 parallel threads.

lessons.question: What does query parallelism use to improve performance?

lessons.title: Enabling Parallelism
lessons.content: Use hints or settings. Example: SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 4; (PostgreSQL) enables parallel execution for scans.

lessons.title: Parallel Table Scans
lessons.content: Parallelism speeds up large table scans. Example: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Orders; may use parallel workers if enabled.

lessons.title: Parallel Joins
lessons.content: Parallelize joins for large datasets. Example: SELECT /*+ PARALLEL */ * FROM Orders o JOIN Customers c ON o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID; (Oracle).

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Parallelism increases CPU usage. Use for large datasets, not small queries.

lessons.title: Limitations
lessons.content: Parallelism may not apply to DML (INSERT/UPDATE) or small tables. Check DBMS support.

lessons.question: Does parallelism apply to INSERT statements?

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: Parallelism is used for data warehousing, large reports, or analytical queries.

lessons.title: DBMS Support
lessons.content: Oracle, PostgreSQL, SQL Server support parallelism; MySQL has limited support. Check documentation.

lessons.title: Range Partitioning Strategy
lessons.content: Partition by ranges for ordered data. Example: CREATE TABLE Sales (SaleID INT, SaleDate DATE) PARTITION BY RANGE (SaleDate) (PARTITION p0 VALUES LESS THAN ('2023-01-01'), PARTITION p1 VALUES LESS THAN ('2024-01-01')); (PostgreSQL).

lessons.question: What is range partitioning best for?

lessons.title: List Partitioning Strategy
lessons.content: Partition by specific values. Example: PARTITION BY LIST (Region) (PARTITION p0 VALUES IN ('North', 'South'), PARTITION p1 VALUES IN ('East', 'West')); (PostgreSQL).

lessons.title: Hash Partitioning Strategy
lessons.content: Distribute data evenly with hash. Example: PARTITION BY HASH (CustomerID) PARTITIONS 4; (PostgreSQL).

lessons.title: Subpartitioning
lessons.content: Combine strategies. Example: PARTITION BY RANGE (SaleDate) SUBPARTITION BY HASH (CustomerID) (PARTITION p0 VALUES LESS THAN ('2024-01-01')); (Oracle).

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Choose partitioning keys that align with query patterns to avoid full scans.

lessons.question: What should partitioning keys align with?

lessons.title: Maintenance
lessons.content: Manage partitions with ALTER TABLE. Example: ALTER TABLE Sales DETACH PARTITION p0; (PostgreSQL).

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: Partitioning strategies are used for time-series data, geographic data, or large-scale analytics.

lessons.question: What are partitioning strategies used for?

lessons.title: DBMS Support
lessons.content: PostgreSQL, Oracle support advanced partitioning; SQL Server uses partition functions; MySQL has basic support.

lessons.title: Conditional Aggregates
lessons.content: Aggregate with conditions. Example: SELECT Category, SUM(CASE WHEN Region = 'North' THEN Sales ELSE 0 END) AS NorthSales FROM Orders GROUP BY Category;

lessons.question: What does CASE in aggregates allow?

lessons.title: ROLLUP
lessons.content: Create subtotals with ROLLUP. Example: SELECT Region, Category, SUM(Sales) FROM Orders GROUP BY ROLLUP(Region, Category);

lessons.title: CUBE
lessons.content: Generate all combinations of aggregates. Example: SELECT Region, Category, SUM(Sales) FROM Orders GROUP BY CUBE(Region, Category);

lessons.title: GROUPING SETS
lessons.content: Define specific groupings. Example: SELECT Region, Category, SUM(Sales) FROM Orders GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((Region), (Category));

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Use indexes on GROUP BY columns to speed up aggregations.

lessons.title: NULL Handling
lessons.content: Use COALESCE for NULLs. Example: SELECT COALESCE(Region, 'Total'), SUM(Sales) FROM Orders GROUP BY ROLLUP(Region);

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: Advanced aggregations are used for financial reports, dashboards, or multi-dimensional analysis.

lessons.question: What are advanced aggregations used for?

lessons.title: DBMS Support
lessons.content: ROLLUP, CUBE, GROUPING SETS are supported in PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle; MySQL supports WITH ROLLUP.

lessons.title: SQL in ML Workflows
lessons.content: SQL prepares data for ML. Example: SELECT CustomerID, AVG(Total) AS AvgSpend FROM Orders GROUP BY CustomerID; for feature engineering.

lessons.question: What does SQL do in ML workflows?

lessons.title: Feature Engineering
lessons.content: Create features with SQL. Example: SELECT CustomerID, COUNT(*) AS OrderCount, SUM(Total) AS TotalSpend FROM Orders GROUP BY CustomerID;

lessons.question: What is feature engineering in SQL?

lessons.title: Window Functions for ML
lessons.content: Use window functions for features. Example: SELECT CustomerID, Total, AVG(Total) OVER (PARTITION BY Region) AS RegionAvg FROM Orders;

lessons.question: What can window functions create for ML?

lessons.title: Data Sampling
lessons.content: Sample data for ML. Example: SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE RANDOM() < 0.1; (PostgreSQL) for 10% random sample.

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Use materialized views or temporary tables for complex ML feature queries to avoid recomputation.

lessons.question: What avoids recomputation in ML queries?

lessons.title: Integration with ML Tools
lessons.content: Export SQL data to ML tools. Example: COPY (SELECT * FROM Features) TO 'features.csv' CSV; (PostgreSQL).

lessons.question: What exports SQL data to ML tools?

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: SQL for ML is used for customer segmentation, churn prediction, or recommendation systems.

lessons.question: What is SQL for ML used for?

lessons.title: DBMS Support
lessons.content: PostgreSQL’s MADlib, SQL Server’s ML Services, Oracle’s OML support ML in SQL.

lessons.title: What Are Cross-Database Queries?
lessons.content: Query across databases. Example: SELECT * FROM db1.dbo.Orders o JOIN db2.dbo.Customers c ON o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID; (SQL Server).

lessons.title: Database Links
lessons.content: Use database links in Oracle. Example: CREATE DATABASE LINK remote_db CONNECT TO user IDENTIFIED BY pass USING 'remote'; SELECT * FROM Orders@remote_db;

lessons.question: What does a database link do in Oracle?

lessons.title: Foreign Data Wrappers
lessons.content: Use FDW in PostgreSQL. Example: CREATE FOREIGN TABLE remote_orders (OrderID INT, Total DECIMAL) SERVER remote_server;

lessons.question: What does FDW do in PostgreSQL?

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Minimize cross-database joins due to network latency. Localize data if possible.

lessons.title: Security
lessons.content: Secure cross-database access with roles. Example: GRANT SELECT ON remote_orders TO analyst; (PostgreSQL).

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: Cross-database queries are used for distributed systems, data integration, or reporting across databases.

lessons.question: What are cross-database queries used for?

lessons.title: DBMS Support
lessons.content: SQL Server uses linked servers, Oracle uses database links, PostgreSQL uses FDW. MySQL has limited support.

lessons.title: Monitoring
lessons.content: Monitor query performance across databases with EXPLAIN or equivalent tools.

lessons.title: What is Database Replication?
lessons.content: Replication copies data to another database. Example: CREATE SUBSCRIPTION sub1 CONNECTION 'host=remote dbname=prod' PUBLICATION pub1; (PostgreSQL).

lessons.title: Read Replicas
lessons.content: Read replicas handle read-only queries. Example: Set up a streaming replica in PostgreSQL for load balancing.

lessons.title: Synchronous Replication
lessons.content: Synchronous replication ensures data consistency. Example: SET synchronous_commit = on; (PostgreSQL).

lessons.title: Asynchronous Replication
lessons.content: Asynchronous replication allows lag. Example: Configure log shipping in SQL Server for async replication.

lessons.title: Failover
lessons.content: Failover switches to a replica. Example: ALTER SYSTEM FAILOVER TO replica_host; (PostgreSQL with tools like Patroni).

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Use read replicas to offload read queries, reducing primary server load.

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: Replication is used for high availability, load balancing, or disaster recovery.

lessons.title: DBMS Support
lessons.content: PostgreSQL uses streaming replication, SQL Server uses Always On, Oracle uses Data Guard.

lessons.title: SQL for Big Data
lessons.content: SQL queries large datasets in big data systems. Example: SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) FROM events GROUP BY user_id; in Apache Spark SQL.

lessons.question: What does SQL query in big data systems?

lessons.title: Distributed Queries
lessons.content: Run SQL on distributed systems. Example: SELECT * FROM hive_table WHERE date = '2023-01-01'; (Apache Hive).

lessons.question: What do distributed queries run on?

lessons.title: Partitioning in Big Data
lessons.content: Partition data for scalability. Example: CREATE TABLE events (user_id INT, date DATE) PARTITIONED BY (date); (Hive).

lessons.question: What does partitioning improve in big data?

lessons.title: Integration with Tools
lessons.content: Use SQL with big data tools. Example: Spark SQL integrates with DataFrames for large-scale processing.

lessons.question: What does Spark SQL integrate with?

lessons.title: Performance Tip
lessons.content: Use columnar storage formats like Parquet or ORC for faster queries in big data systems.

lessons.question: What improves query performance in big data?

lessons.title: Window Functions in Big Data
lessons.content: Use window functions for analytics. Example: SELECT user_id, SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY date) FROM transactions; (Spark SQL).

lessons.question: What are window functions used for in big data?

lessons.title: Use Cases
lessons.content: SQL for big data is used for log analysis, real-time analytics, or large-scale reporting.

lessons.question: What is SQL for big data used for?

lessons.title: Tools
lessons.content: Popular tools include Apache Spark SQL, Hive, Presto, and BigQuery. Check compatibility.
